story.headline: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates to 4.00% at 6:00 AM CT, its first rise since 2023. Overnight, gold climbed to about $4,135 and oil kept falling.

reads.policy: Most big central banks still lean toward higher rates, and the Bank of England is set to raise on Thursday. Bank of Japan minutes backed more rises, and bets on a December Fed hike barely moved after the US elections. Currencies now move on hints about the next step, not on hikes already expected.
reads.growth: Australia's exports rose strongly, giving it its biggest trade surplus in seven months. US figures this week have been mixed but healthy, and a Democratic Congress is expected to spend less, which could slow US growth next year. US jobs figures on Thursday and Friday are the next real read.
reads.inflation: Oil's slide on hopes of an end to the Iran war, if it lasts, would ease price pressure almost everywhere and take some heat off central banks. For now inflation is still high in the US, the UK and the euro area, so the hikes already planned stay on track.
reads.risk: Markets stayed mostly calm overnight after Wall Street's big rally, though chip stocks fell in Seoul and Tokyo on worries about tighter US rules on AI. The franc firmed and gold climbed, but on a weaker dollar more than on fear.
reads.tot: Oil fell for a fourth day on bets the Iran war winds down, cutting the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. Exporters like Canada and Australia earn less, though Australia's latest trade figures still showed strong gas and metals sales.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and they are also betting against the euro and the kiwi, while real money investors bet for the euro. Their large bets on gold have been shrinking. New figures arrive Friday.
reads.fiscal: Democrats now control both houses of Congress, so President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which takes some support away from the dollar. Canada presents its federal budget on Thursday afternoon, and France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and strong US figures have made a December hike look likely. Democrats' win in Congress weighed on the dollar but barely moved those hike bets.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and the jobs market shows the economy can take higher rates.
fed.watch: Weekly jobless claims at 7:30 AM CT Thursday and the October jobs report at 7:30 AM CT Friday: strong figures would all but lock in a December hike.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and Governor Tiff Macklem says more may be needed. But the economy has stalled and oil just fell sharply, so the bank says it will move carefully.
boc.priced: December: another hike slightly more likely than not.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation, which the bank sees near 3.5% by year-end, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Governor Tiff Macklem before the Senate banking committee at 9:30 AM CT and Canada's federal budget at 3:00 PM CT Thursday, then October jobs figures on Friday.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, and weak job figures since then have cut bets on a December hike. That leaves the kiwi with less support going into Saturday's election.
rbnz.priced: December: hike still slightly more likely than not, but less so after weak jobs data.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, but unemployment has risen to its highest since 2015, which eases pressure on wages and prices.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand's general election on Saturday, November 7, and any comments from the bank before its December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29 and pointed to a December hike. Euro-area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, as expected, which keeps that plan on track.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation to about double the 2% goal, though underlying prices are steadier, so the bank has no reason to rush beyond one hike.
ecb.watch: ECB President Christine Lagarde's speech at noon CT Thursday and whether energy prices keep falling before the December 17 decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, with one member voting to hike, and minutes of its September meeting show the board backs more rises. A December hike looks likely and would give the yen, near 158 per dollar, more support.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy, and one member has said the pace of hikes may need to quicken.
boj.watch: Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech at 10:00 AM CT Friday, Japanese wage and price figures, and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three of nine members wanted to wait and Governor Michele Bullock said it was time to take stock. Markets now expect its next move, in time, to be a cut.
rba.priced: December: no move expected; some cuts priced by the end of next year.
rba.why: Inflation has run hotter than the bank expected and will stay above its target until late 2027, but a weakening job market argues for caution.
rba.watch: Australian jobs and inflation figures before the December 8 decision, and the Chinese yuan, which the Aussie often follows.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates to 4.00% at 6:00 AM CT Thursday, its first hike since 2023, and the debate is already about December. The pound eased overnight from a seven-week high as traders waited.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, and factory prices are climbing faster.
boe.watch: The vote split and Monetary Policy Report at 6:00 AM CT, and Governor Andrew Bailey's news conference at 6:30 AM CT: any hint about December matters more than the hike.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October on fuel, which makes another cut less likely, though not a hike.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Fuel lifted Swiss inflation to its highest since late 2023, but underlying prices stayed calm, so the bank has no reason to raise rates.
snb.watch: Chairman Martin Schlegel's speech at 6:40 AM CT Thursday, especially anything on the franc's strength, and the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the upper half of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Democrats' win of both houses of Congress, which points to less government spending, now weighs on it.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, after strong jobs figures.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, though oil's sharp fall could start to ease it.
notes.fiscal: Democrats won both houses of Congress, so President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which takes some support from the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is uneven, energy imports cost more, and France's debt worries weigh on it. A likely European Central Bank hike in December and a weaker US dollar give it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth is uneven: France shrank over the summer, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, mostly on energy, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out, though oil's sharp fall eases that bill.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: Two of the three big rating firms now have France on negative outlook, which keeps investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound tops the board because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, inflation is high and business surveys are strong.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on Thursday, November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, with factories at their busiest in two years, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators betting heavily against the pound, so a firm Bank of England could force them to buy it back.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. It still gains when markets get nervous, as they did after the US midterm results.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is still far below others', but minutes of its September meeting show the board backs more rises, pointing to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, as it did when chip stocks slid in Seoul and Tokyo, though calm on Wall Street limits that lift.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country; oil's sharp fall eases that.
notes.positioning: Broad measures show speculators holding unusually big bets on the yen, which could unwind fast if it weakens.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, mostly on fuel, but underlying prices are calm, so the Swiss National Bank still has no reason to raise rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, and it firmed again as chip stocks slid in Asia, though hopes for an end to the Iran war trim that demand.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because Australia’s rates are now the highest among major economies and it sells resources abroad. But the central bank hinted it may pause after its latest hike, and a weakening job market is a drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest of the major banks, but it dropped its hint of more.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected and is set to stay high until late 2027.
notes.tot: Australia sells gas and metals abroad, and its trade surplus hit a seven-month high in September, though oil's sharp fall trims what energy earns.
notes.positioning: Real money investors hold some of their biggest bets against the Aussie in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and oil still brings money in. Growth is the soft spot, and oil's sharp fall on hopes of an end to the Iran war trims its support.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and its governor says more may be needed, so a December hike is slightly more likely than not.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so crude brings money in, but oil has fallen four days in a row on hopes of an end to the Iran war, which cuts that income.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits in the middle of the board: New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, and unemployment has now risen to its highest since 2015. Firm dairy prices limit the damage, and Saturday's election adds uncertainty.

notes.growth: Unemployment rose to 5.7%, the highest since 2015, and jobs fell, which weakens the case for a December rate hike.
notes.tot: Dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, have risen at three auctions in a row, bringing money into the country.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so good news could force them to buy it back.
